executive_summary: On February 3, 2026, the Dutch parliament held its 38th session to debate the coalition agreement of a three-party government formed by D66, VVD, and CDA, with D66 leader Jetten as Prime Minister. The 76 decisions covered major policy reforms including healthcare changes, defense spending increases, pension age adjustments, and tax measures, with significant opposition from PVV and GroenLinks-PvdA over fiscal burden distribution and broken campaign promises.

main_topics.summary: The session centered on ratification of a three-party coalition agreement between D66, VVD, and CDA (66 parliamentary seats total), with Jetten leading the government. The coalition presented its policy framework addressing housing, healthcare, security, education, and environmental transition. This minority government will require support from other parties on specific issues.

party_positions.D66 (Jetten): Strongly supports the agreement as pragmatic solution addressing major national challenges; emphasizes cooperation over ideological purity and highlights achievements across coalition partners' priorities
party_positions.VVD: Coalition partner supporting the agreement (specific positions not detailed in provided data)
party_positions.CDA: Coalition partner supporting the agreement (specific positions not detailed in provided data)
party_positions.PVV (Wilders): Vehemently opposes, claiming the coalition breaks election promises, excessively taxes citizens, cuts benefits unfairly, and is insufficiently strict on asylum policy
party_positions.GroenLinks-PvdA (Klaver): Critical of fiscal burden distribution, arguing wealthy citizens are protected while working-class citizens bear costs; notes minority status will force coalition to negotiate for parliamentary support
party_positions.DENK (Van Baarle): Concerned about cumulative tax burden from multiple new costs affecting citizens
party_positions.SGP (Stoffer): Establishes red line on medical ethics as condition for future cooperation
party_positions.Volt (Dassen): Questions tax fairness and advocates for wealth transfer taxation and addressing inherited wealth inequality
party_positions.50PLUS (Struijs): Objects to breaking previous government's pension accord, emphasizing governmental reliability

main_topics.outcome: Coalition agreement formally adopted; government formation completed with Jetten as Prime Minister; minority status (66 of 150 seats) requires coalition to build majorities per-issue with opposition parties

main_topics.summary: Significant proposed changes to healthcare financing and social security systems, including increases to patient copayments (eigen risico) and benefit adjustments. The government proposed increasing copayment with compensation mechanisms for vulnerable populations.

party_positions.D66 (Jetten): Defends healthcare reforms as necessary and includes compensation measures (€350 million annually for vulnerable groups, €150 per-treatment cap) to protect those most in need
party_positions.PVV (Wilders): Opposes as harmful to citizens despite campaign promises
party_positions.Opposition parties: Critical of cumulative costs and burden on working-class citizens

main_topics.outcome: Own risk (eigen risico) healthcare contribution increased to €460 with €150 per-treatment cap; €350 million annual compensation approved for vulnerable groups; healthcare wait times reduction established as priority

main_topics.summary: Controversial decision to link AOW (state pension) age to life expectancy starting from 2033, representing a break from previous government agreements and shifting retirement expectations.

party_positions.D66 (Jetten): Argues adjustment necessary for long-term sustainability of pension system despite breaking previous accord
party_positions.50PLUS (Struijs): Strongly opposes, emphasizing importance of governmental reliability and keeping pension promises
party_positions.Opposition: General concern about breaking previous agreements

main_topics.outcome: AOW retirement age increase starting from 2033, linked to life expectancy (implementation deferred to future); €350 million compensation for vulnerable groups approved

main_topics.summary: Major policy shift committing Netherlands to significant defense budget increases to meet NATO's 2% GDP spending norm, funded partly through new 'vrijheidsbijdrage' (freedom contribution) tax.

party_positions.D66 (Jetten): Supports €19.3 billion additional defense spending as responsibility to NATO alliance and European security
party_positions.Coalition: Unified support for defense spending increases
party_positions.Opposition: Some concerns about funding mechanisms and tax burden (noted by multiple parties)

main_topics.outcome: €19.3 billion additional defense spending committed to meet 2% NATO norm; new 'vrijheidsbijdrage' tax introduced to fund defense and other priorities; defense established as major budget priority

main_topics.summary: Debate over multiple new tax measures and their cumulative burden on citizens, including healthcare copayments, NATO tax, sugar tax, fuel duty increases, and benefit cuts.

party_positions.D66 (Jetten): Defends tax measures as necessary investments with compensation for vulnerable populations; argues progressive elements protect lower-income citizens
party_positions.DENK (Van Baarle): Critical of cumulative burden from multiple new costs (healthcare copayment, NATO tax, sugar tax, fuel duty, benefits cuts)
party_positions.Volt (Dassen): Advocates for progressive taxation including wealth transfer taxes and addressing inherited wealth inequality
party_positions.PVV (Wilders): Condemns as excessive taxation harming citizens while protecting wealthy
party_positions.GroenLinks-PvdA (Klaver): Argues wealthy citizens are protected while working-class citizens bear disproportionate costs

main_topics.outcome: Multiple tax measures implemented including NATO 'vrijheidsbijdrage', healthcare copayment increases, sugar tax, and fuel duty increases; €350 million compensation approved for vulnerable groups; debate continues on progressive taxation

main_topics.summary: Housing shortage identified as major policy priority with coalition commitment to increased construction and policy reforms to address affordability and availability.

party_positions.D66 (Jetten): Prioritizes housing as central to government agenda; emphasizes pragmatic approaches to accelerate construction

political_dynamics: The meeting revealed a sharply divided parliament. The three-coalition partners (D66, VVD, CDA) present a unified front supporting pragmatic governance and policy packages, but their 66-seat minority requires negotiation with opposition parties per issue. PVV under Wilders emerges as the strongest opposition voice, using heated rhetoric about broken campaign promises and excessive taxation. GroenLinks-PvdA adopts a more measured critical stance, focusing on fiscal burden distribution and inequality. Smaller parties (SGP, DENK, Volt, 50PLUS) establish specific red lines or policy priorities as conditions for future support, giving them leverage despite smaller representation. The coalition's minority status creates significant incentive for negotiation and compromise on major legislation. The debate reveals fundamental disagreements on taxation philosophy, pension policy continuity, and social security priorities between governing coalition and opposition.
